title: Japanese, from the first word
description: A small original starter collection for first greetings and hiragana. The full beginner course is still being written.
review_note: Original technical starter slice. Internal consistency reviewed; independent qualified Japanese-language review is pending. Full stage coverage is not claimed. Original ten-topic vocabulary expansion remains draft; independent Japanese review and complete 500+1500 lexical coverage are still pending.

concepts.title: Greetings
concepts.explanation: Choose a greeting for the time and situation. こんにちは is used during the day.

concepts.title: Polite first exchanges
concepts.explanation: です and ございます help create polite everyday exchanges.

concepts.title: Hiragana sound patterns
concepts.explanation: A normal kana generally represents one mora. Small っ and long vowels affect timing.

concepts.title: Small kana change the sound
concepts.explanation: きゃ is one combined mora (kya); きや has two morae (ki-ya). Small ゃ/ゅ/ょ combine after an i-row kana. Small っ marks a held consonant before the next sound: きって (stamp), not きて. Audio examples arrive with audio practice.

concepts.title: The independent ん
concepts.explanation: ん counts as one mora. It can occur inside or at the end of a word: ほん (book). Its sound changes with neighboring sounds; do not delete it or confuse it with a following vowel.

concepts.title: Keep long vowels
concepts.explanation: Vowel length can distinguish words. おばさん (aunt) and おばあさん (grandmother) differ in length. In hiragana, long vowels use authored spellings: おかあさん and がっこう. Katakana commonly uses ー: コーヒー. Do not shorten these spellings. Audio contrasts are not available yet.

concepts.title: Voicing and similar shapes
concepts.explanation: Dakuten changes a kana: か→が and は→ば. Handakuten gives は→ぱ. Katakana シ/ツ and ソ/ン have similar shapes; notice the orientation and placement of the short strokes. A font sample is a reading aid, not stroke-order instruction.

concepts.title: Read a kanji inside a word
concepts.explanation: Kanji readings depend on the word. 日 is に in 日本 (にほん), but にち in 日曜日 (にちようび). Study the whole contextual word. One recognition answer does not prove every reading or handwriting skill.

concepts.title: は · Topic in a polite introduction
concepts.explanation: は marks what we are talking about. In 私はミナです, 私 is the topic; it does not mean every subject always takes は.

concepts.title: が · Identify what is present
concepts.explanation: が identifies the person or thing being introduced: 駅があります means there is a station. This scoped existence pattern does not make が interchangeable with topic は.

concepts.title: を · Object of an action
concepts.explanation: を marks the object of actions such as drinking: 水を飲みます. It is read お here. A place of action takes で in the pattern taught next.

concepts.title: に · A specific time or destination
concepts.explanation: に marks a specific clock time with an action: 三時に行きます. In 学校に行きます it instead marks a destination. Context and the verb determine the use; not all time expressions need に.

concepts.title: で · Place where an action happens
concepts.explanation: で marks where an action occurs: 学校で勉強します. Compare 学校に行きます, going to school. Existence uses a different pattern: 学校に先生がいます.

concepts.title: へ · Direction of movement
concepts.explanation: へ marks direction with movement: 学校へ行きます. Read the particle え. に can mark the destination with this verb, but it cannot freely replace へ or other particles in every sentence.

concepts.title: Katakana words in context
concepts.explanation: Preserve authored katakana spelling and vowel length in familiar nouns.

concepts.title: Point to people and things
concepts.explanation: これ・それ・あれ identify things in a shared situation; this guide teaches scoped noun sentences.

concepts.title: Clock times and item counts
concepts.explanation: Learn the contextual clock and counter readings explicitly taught in each example.

concepts.title: A polite counter request
concepts.explanation: Use the authored object + を + ください pattern and context-specific request alternatives.

concepts.title: Polite routines and past actions
concepts.explanation: Distinguish the taught ます／ました／ません／ませんでした forms in a stated time context.

concepts.title: Descriptions and preferences
concepts.explanation: Contrast the taught い-adjective negative and the separate 好きです pattern.

concepts.title: Invite and reply politely
concepts.explanation: Recognize a polite ませんか invitation and task-specific acceptance or refusal.

units.title: First sounds and greetings
units.description: Start with a few useful phrases and notice how Japanese sounds.
units.guide:
こんにちは is a daytime greeting. Its final は is pronounced wa; keep the conventional spelling.

ありがとう expresses thanks; ありがとうございます adds politeness. The longer phrase is useful with people you do not know well.

A name followed by です is a polite introduction. Japanese can leave “I” unstated when the context is clear.

units.title: Hiragana foundations
units.description: Read the vowel and k rows, then notice small kana and voicing.
units.guide:
The first vowel row is あ (a), い (i), う (u), え (e), お (o). The simple words あい and いえ combine these kana.

The k row is か・き・く・け・こ. In かお (face), both か and the vowel お keep their sounds.

Dakuten changes か to が. Small っ marks a pause before the next consonant: きって differs from きて. In がっこう, こう has a long vowel.

units.title: Katakana and familiar words
units.description: Learn the basic katakana set, combinations, loanwords, and long vowels.
units.guide: Katakana commonly writes borrowed words. The mark ー extends the preceding vowel: コーヒー is koohii. The small vowel in ティ changes the combination; it is not an extra full-size イ. Learn each word’s authored spelling rather than replacing letters one by one from English. Read コーヒー as a whole word before trying its written form.

units.title: People and things
units.description: Use は, です, questions and demonstratives in simple descriptions.
units.guide: これ points to something near the speaker, それ near the listener, and あれ farther from both. In これは本です, は introduces the topic and is pronounced wa. Add か after です to ask a polite question. この needs a following noun: この本. Before the checks, read 本 as ほん (book) and 何 as なん in 何ですか.

units.title: Numbers, time, and purchases
units.description: Use explicitly taught number, time, date and counter readings.
units.guide: Use 時 after an hour number: 三時 is さんじ, 四時 is よじ, 七時 is しちじ and 九時 is くじ in this beginner set. A specific clock time can take に: 三時に行きます (I will go at three). 今日 and 毎日 do not normally take に in this use. Counters change readings; 一つ is ひとつ. This guide teaches only these examples, not every date or counter.

units.title: Food and ordering
units.description: Use polite requests, を and common menu words.
units.guide: Use noun + を + ください for a polite request: 水をください (water, please). 水 is みず; を is the object marker, normally pronounced o. A short shop request can also use お願いします. These are task-specific alternatives, not a claim that every sentence with ください can be replaced by お願いします. Read the model before the checks.

units.title: Places and directions
units.description: Use に, で and へ in taught location and movement contexts.
units.guide: 駅はどこですか asks where the station is; 駅 is えき and どこ means where. With 行きます (go), 駅に行きます names the destination and 駅へ行きます emphasizes direction. Both fit “go to the station” in this scoped task. In 駅で待ちます, で instead names where waiting happens; 待ちます is まちます. Read the three complete patterns before choosing a particle.

units.title: Daily routines
units.description: Describe schedules using polite present, past and negative forms.
units.guide: Start with the complete polite verb forms: 勉強します (study), 勉強しました (studied), 勉強しません (do not/will not study), and 勉強しませんでした (did not study). 勉強 is べんきょう. The nonpast form covers routines or future actions depending on context. 昨日 (きのう) supplies a past context. 家で names where studying happens; 家 is いえ here. Read these forms before trying the checks.

units.title: Descriptions and preferences
units.description: Use introductory adjectives, preferences and taught comparisons.
units.guide: 高い (たかい) can mean expensive or tall, depending on the noun and situation. For this price task, 高いです means it is expensive and 高くないです means it is not expensive. 好き (すき) describes liking; it is not an い-adjective. Use the taught pattern お茶が好きです (I like tea), with お茶 read おちゃ. Do not apply 高くない mechanically to 好き.

units.title: Everyday connections
units.description: Write short messages, make invitations and revisit practical exchanges.
units.guide: Verb + ませんか can invite someone: 一緒にお茶を飲みませんか (Would you like to have tea together?). 一緒に is いっしょに and 飲みます is のみます. はい、飲みましょう accepts this invitation. すみません、今日はちょっと softly declines without giving a full reason; 今日 is きょう. These examples model two valid intentions, so a decline is not graded as a mistaken acceptance.

grammar_notes.title: A polite first introduction
grammar_notes.explanation: Use a name followed by です to introduce yourself politely. The speaker can be left unstated when the context is clear.
grammar_notes.register_note: Polite first meeting; alternatives depend on context.
common_mistakes: です follows the name in this introduction; do not add an unnecessary English-style subject to every sentence.
grammar_notes.culture_note: はじめまして is used at a first meeting; later greetings depend on the time and relationship.

grammar_notes.title: は · Topic in a polite introduction
grammar_notes.explanation: は marks what we are talking about. In 私はミナです, 私 is the topic; it does not mean every subject always takes は.
grammar_notes.register_note: Polite everyday examples. Plain speech and broader contrasts need separate instruction. Draft: independent Japanese review pending.
common_mistakes: The topic marker は fits this self-introduction. が can identify a subject in other contexts; this task explicitly introduces the speaker as the topic.
grammar_notes.culture_note: These examples use polite forms. Choose expressions for the relationship and setting; politeness is not a judgment of the speaker.

grammar_notes.title: が · Identify what is present
grammar_notes.explanation: が identifies the person or thing being introduced: 駅があります means there is a station. This scoped existence pattern does not make が interchangeable with topic は.
grammar_notes.register_note: Polite everyday examples. Plain speech and broader contrasts need separate instruction. Draft: independent Japanese review pending.
common_mistakes: In this existence pattern, が identifies the thing that exists. を marks an action’s object in the scoped pattern taught here.
grammar_notes.culture_note: These examples use polite forms. Choose expressions for the relationship and setting; politeness is not a judgment of the speaker.

grammar_notes.title: を · Object of an action
grammar_notes.explanation: を marks the object of actions such as drinking: 水を飲みます. It is read お here. A place of action takes で in the pattern taught next.
grammar_notes.register_note: Polite everyday examples. Plain speech and broader contrasts need separate instruction. Draft: independent Japanese review pending.
common_mistakes: 水 is the object of drinking, so use を. で can mark the place where the action happens.
grammar_notes.culture_note: These examples use polite forms. Choose expressions for the relationship and setting; politeness is not a judgment of the speaker.

grammar_notes.title: に · A specific time or destination
grammar_notes.explanation: に marks a specific clock time with an action: 三時に行きます. In 学校に行きます it instead marks a destination. Context and the verb determine the use; not all time expressions need に.
grammar_notes.register_note: Polite everyday examples. Plain speech and broader contrasts need separate instruction. Draft: independent Japanese review pending.
common_mistakes: 三時 is a specific clock time. に marks when the action occurs here; で does not express this meaning.
grammar_notes.culture_note: These examples use polite forms. Choose expressions for the relationship and setting; politeness is not a judgment of the speaker.

grammar_notes.title: で · Place where an action happens
grammar_notes.explanation: で marks where an action occurs: 学校で勉強します. Compare 学校に行きます, going to school. Existence uses a different pattern: 学校に先生がいます.

examples.reading: がっこうでべんきょうします。

grammar_notes.register_note: Polite everyday examples. Plain speech and broader contrasts need separate instruction. Draft: independent Japanese review pending.
common_mistakes: で marks the location of studying. Compare 学校に行きます, where に marks the destination.
grammar_notes.culture_note: These examples use polite forms. Choose expressions for the relationship and setting; politeness is not a judgment of the speaker.

grammar_notes.title: へ · Direction of movement
grammar_notes.explanation: へ marks direction with movement: 学校へ行きます. Read the particle え. に can mark the destination with this verb, but it cannot freely replace へ or other particles in every sentence.
grammar_notes.register_note: Polite everyday examples. Plain speech and broader contrasts need separate instruction. Draft: independent Japanese review pending.
common_mistakes: へ marks direction with movement and is read え. に is also a destination alternative with 行きます; を is not the direction marker in this task.
grammar_notes.culture_note: These examples use polite forms. Choose expressions for the relationship and setting; politeness is not a judgment of the speaker.

grammar_notes.title: Read the marks as part of the word
grammar_notes.explanation: A basic kana usually contributes one mora. Small ゃ・ゅ・ょ combine with a preceding i-row kana; small っ holds the next consonant for a mora. ん has its own mora. Preserve dakuten, handakuten and vowel length. For these examples, compare きゃ with きや and おばさん with おばあさん. Sound guidance is text-based here; real reviewed audio remains pending.

examples.surface: きゃ・きや・きって・きて
おばさん・おばあさん・ほん

grammar_notes.register_note: Script patterns apply across registers; examples here teach spelling distinctions.
common_mistakes: Do not enlarge small kana, drop っ or ん, or remove long vowels when typing.
grammar_notes.culture_note: Kana practice prepares later words; a recognition result does not prove handwriting or pronunciation.

grammar_notes.title: Katakana words keep their length
grammar_notes.explanation: Katakana commonly writes borrowed words. The mark ー extends the preceding vowel: コーヒー is koohii. The small vowel in ティ changes the combination; it is not an extra full-size イ. Learn each word’s authored spelling rather than replacing letters one by one from English. Read コーヒー as a whole word before trying its written form.
grammar_notes.register_note: コーヒー is a neutral noun. Add a polite request when ordering.
common_mistakes: コヒ drops the long vowels in コーヒー. Katakana spelling is not English spelling.
grammar_notes.culture_note: Katakana is also used for emphasis and some names; “katakana means foreign” is not a complete rule.

grammar_notes.title: Name a thing and ask about it
grammar_notes.explanation: これ points to something near the speaker, それ near the listener, and あれ farther from both. In これは本です, は introduces the topic and is pronounced wa. Add か after です to ask a polite question. この needs a following noun: この本. Before the checks, read 本 as ほん (book) and 何 as なん in 何ですか.
grammar_notes.register_note: です／ですか are polite patterns suitable for a first exchange.
common_mistakes: これ can stand alone; この must describe a noun. Do not put か before です in this pattern.
grammar_notes.culture_note: Use the shared situation to choose a demonstrative; it is not a fixed English “this/that” substitution.

grammar_notes.title: Clock time and one item
grammar_notes.explanation: Use 時 after an hour number: 三時 is さんじ, 四時 is よじ, 七時 is しちじ and 九時 is くじ in this beginner set. A specific clock time can take に: 三時に行きます (I will go at three). 今日 and 毎日 do not normally take に in this use. Counters change readings; 一つ is ひとつ. This guide teaches only these examples, not every date or counter.
grammar_notes.register_note: 行きます and ください keep these short exchanges polite.
common_mistakes: Do not read 四時 as よんじ in this set. Counter readings need their own contexts.
grammar_notes.culture_note: A price, a clock time and an item count use different forms; ask for clarification when needed.

grammar_notes.title: Ask for something at a counter
grammar_notes.explanation: Use noun + を + ください for a polite request: 水をください (water, please). 水 is みず; を is the object marker, normally pronounced o. A short shop request can also use お願いします. These are task-specific alternatives, not a claim that every sentence with ください can be replaced by お願いします. Read the model before the checks.
grammar_notes.register_note: These requests are polite. Avoid the bare noun alone when the task asks for a polite request.
common_mistakes: で does not mark the requested object in 水をください. Write the particle を, even though it sounds like お.
grammar_notes.culture_note: A brief すみません can get staff attention; language and service customs vary by setting.

grammar_notes.title: Ask where, then name a destination
grammar_notes.explanation: 駅はどこですか asks where the station is; 駅 is えき and どこ means where. With 行きます (go), 駅に行きます names the destination and 駅へ行きます emphasizes direction. Both fit “go to the station” in this scoped task. In 駅で待ちます, で instead names where waiting happens; 待ちます is まちます. Read the three complete patterns before choosing a particle.
grammar_notes.register_note: ですか／ます are polite forms for asking a stranger.
common_mistakes: Do not use the movement-destination explanation as a rule for every に. で marks the action location in the waiting example.
grammar_notes.culture_note: すみません、駅はどこですか。 gives a brief polite way to approach someone; asking does not guarantee an answer.

grammar_notes.title: A routine, yesterday, and a negative
grammar_notes.explanation: Start with the complete polite verb forms: 勉強します (study), 勉強しました (studied), 勉強しません (do not/will not study), and 勉強しませんでした (did not study). 勉強 is べんきょう. The nonpast form covers routines or future actions depending on context. 昨日 (きのう) supplies a past context. 家で names where studying happens; 家 is いえ here. Read these forms before trying the checks.
grammar_notes.register_note: These examples stay in polite ます style rather than switching to plain dictionary forms.
common_mistakes: ません is nonpast negative; ませんでした is past negative. Do not add です after these ます-form verbs.
grammar_notes.culture_note: A routine is a useful conversation topic; the speaker can be omitted when context makes it clear.

grammar_notes.title: Describe something and say what you like
grammar_notes.explanation: 高い (たかい) can mean expensive or tall, depending on the noun and situation. For this price task, 高いです means it is expensive and 高くないです means it is not expensive. 好き (すき) describes liking; it is not an い-adjective. Use the taught pattern お茶が好きです (I like tea), with お茶 read おちゃ. Do not apply 高くない mechanically to 好き.
grammar_notes.register_note: です keeps the examples polite. 高くありません is another polite negative, but it is not required in these checks.
common_mistakes: The い-adjective negative is 高くない, not 高いない. 好き is not an い-adjective.
grammar_notes.culture_note: Preferences can be softened according to the situation; this task practices a simple stated preference.

grammar_notes.title: Invite someone and leave a short reply
grammar_notes.explanation: Verb + ませんか can invite someone: 一緒にお茶を飲みませんか (Would you like to have tea together?). 一緒に is いっしょに and 飲みます is のみます. はい、飲みましょう accepts this invitation. すみません、今日はちょっと softly declines without giving a full reason; 今日 is きょう. These examples model two valid intentions, so a decline is not graded as a mistaken acceptance.
grammar_notes.register_note: Use a polite invitation with a new acquaintance; these short models do not cover every relationship.
common_mistakes: ませんか here is an invitation, not simply a statement that someone does not drink. Match an acceptance or decline to the task intention.
grammar_notes.culture_note: ちょっと can soften a refusal. It is context-dependent and does not literally explain the reason.
